svg.text: JWT Security — What Decoding Doesn't Protect You From
A decoded JWT is readable by anyone — these are the real security boundaries
✗ Never trust decoded claims without verifying the signature
Anyone can decode a JWT's payload and read it — Base64URL is not encryption. Anyone can also
forge a fake JWT with any claims they want. Only a valid signature — verified with the secret or
public key — proves the token was issued by your server and hasn't been tampered with.
JWT supports an "alg: none" mode meaning "no signature." Some early libraries would accept a
JWT with alg set to "none" and blindly trust its claims. Modern libraries reject this by default —
but always explicitly configure your verifier to only accept the specific algorithm you expect.
⚠ Storing JWTs in localStorage is vulnerable to XSS
JavaScript running on your page (including from a successful XSS attack) can read anything in
localStorage and exfiltrate the token. Prefer httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies, which are
⚠ JWTs cannot be revoked before they expire
Once issued, a valid JWT remains valid until its exp claim passes — there is no built-in way to
invalidate it early (e.g., on logout or after a password change) without maintaining a server-side
denylist, which reintroduces the statefulness JWTs were meant to avoid. Keep expiry times short.
